strengths: Introduces a novel and intuitive approach to align speech tokenization with text token length via an ASR-initialized aggregator, directly targeting the sequence-length mismatch in joint speech-text modeling.

Achieves very low estimated bitrate (~190 bps) while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality on LibriTTS test-clean, with some evidence of preserved paralinguistic information such as emotion and duration consistency.

Shows that a text LLM can be adapted into a spoken language model with LoRA, yielding reasonable performance on StoryCloze and above-chance acoustic discrimination on SALMON, suggesting practical utility of text-aligned tokens/embeddings.
Provides detailed training setup and uses public models/datasets, which supports potential reproducibility with effort.
weaknesses: Missing critical ablations: no experiments isolate the effect of ASR initialization, the proposed shallow-value cross-attention aggregator, word-level averaging/alignment, RVQ depth/codebook size, or text alignment itself. A simple forced-alignment/pooling baseline is not compared, so the necessity of the proposed method is unclear.

The reconstruction evaluation is confounded and incomplete: a text-only baseline with speaker embedding already achieves similar WER, UTMOS, and speaker similarity, implying the speech tokenization adds only marginal acoustic information. UTMOS exceeding ground truth is suspicious, and the custom metrics are not standard. Evaluation is limited to LibriTTS test-clean, with no in-the-wild or subjective listening tests.

The spoken language modeling evaluation does not convincingly support the claims: TASLM performs below ASR+LLM on StoryCloze and below Spirit LM Expr./pGSLM on several SALMON acoustic dimensions. The S3-token baseline is near chance, possibly due to unfair or poorly tuned joint-modeling setup, and no other speech tokenizers are compared under the same LoRA adaptation protocol.

It is unclear how TASTE is used at inference for a standalone spoken language model: producing text-aligned tokens requires an ASR transcription, so the model is not fully end-to-end or independent of text. This reliance on external ASR/text undermines the claimed ability to listen and speak naturally without cascaded components.

The 'first end-to-end' and 'reconstruction objective' claims are overstated: the encoder is frozen from Distil-Whisper, the target units and vocoder come from CosyVoice/S3, and the vocoder is not trained. The method is better described as a text-conditioned tokenizer/compressor trained to predict S3 units, not an end-to-end speech tokenization from waveform.

Reproducibility and clarity issues remain: no code/model release is mentioned, likelihood/evaluation details for SALMON and StoryCloze are sparse, Algorithm 1 is malformed, and there are numerous typos and notational errors. No qualitative examples or statistical significance tests are provided.
Ethical considerations around speech generation, speaker embedding, voice cloning, and ASR bias are not discussed.

strengths: Tackles the relevant problem of sequence-length mismatch between speech and text tokens in spoken language modeling.
Proposes a text-aligned speech tokenization approach that uses an ASR-initialized encoder-aggregator with text queries and RVQ, enabling dynamic compression.
Achieves very low estimated bitrate (~190 bps) on LibriTTS while maintaining competitive WER/UTMOS and some paralinguistic similarity metrics.
Demonstrates LoRA-based adaptation of a text LLM into an SLM, which is computationally appealing and parameter-efficient.
Reports improvements over some prior SLMs on StoryCloze and competitive acoustic metrics on SALMON.
The use of a reconstruction objective to learn text-aligned speech tokens/embeddings is a reasonable direction.
weaknesses: Tokenization evaluation is very limited: only LibriTTS test-clean clean read speech, with no in-the-wild (e.g., Emilia) or cross-domain evaluation, no human evaluation, and no audio samples.

SLM evaluation lacks controlled comparisons: no same-base-model full fine-tuning baseline, no same-data/S3-token full fine-tuning baseline, and no ablation of LoRA vs full fine-tuning; prior systems use different model sizes and training data.

The 'end-to-end' text-alignment claim is overstated: alignment to LLM tokenization requires a non-learned word-level grouping/averaging/repetition heuristic, and the tokenizer actually aligns to ASR subword tokens, not LLM text tokens.

No ablation studies for key design choices, including the modified aggregator cross-attention, ASR initialization, shallow-value/last-key choices, RVQ layers/codebook size, word-level averaging, and token vs. embedding modeling.

Method and reproducibility are under-specified: Algorithm 1 contains notation errors and unclear procedures, no code/checkpoints are provided, and the pipeline relies on frozen Distil-Whisper, S3 tokens, and an external vocoder.

Speech-tokenization gains may partly stem from text conditioning: the text-only baseline already achieves high UTMOS and speaker similarity, while speech tokens mainly add emotion/duration consistency and still lag in duration consistency.

Reported SLM results are not state-of-the-art and do not clearly establish the claimed competitiveness: TASLM is lower than Spirit LM Expr on several SALMON metrics and below the ASR+LLM topline on StoryCloze, with no variance or significance testing.
Clarity is poor: numerous typos and grammatical errors, inconsistent notation, and non-self-contained figures; ethical implications of speech generation and ASR bias are not discussed.

strengths: Introduces TASTE, a text-aligned speech tokenization and embedding method that directly reduces the speech-text sequence-length mismatch by aligning speech tokens with ASR text tokens during tokenization, without requiring explicit word-level alignments.

The proposed encoder-aggregator-quantizer architecture is technically plausible: it leverages an ASR model as initialization, uses a specialized cross-attention aggregation over shallow and last encoder representations, and applies RVQ to produce discrete text-aligned speech tokens/embeddings.

Speech reconstruction results are promising: TASTE achieves comparable quality and similarity to strong speech tokenizers such as S3 tokens and SpeechTokenizer at a much lower estimated bitrate (~190 bps), while substantially outperforming a text-only baseline on paralinguistic similarity metrics.

The method enables parameter-efficient adaptation of a text LLM into a spoken language model via LoRA, and the word-level grouping/averaging/alignment algorithm provides a practical solution to the ASR-LLM vocabulary mismatch.

The paper evaluates both the tokenization stage and the downstream spoken language modeling stage, reporting competitive results on SALMON and StoryCloze relative to prior full-finetuning SLMs, with a smaller 1B model and LoRA.
The overall approach is clearly motivated and describes an interesting direction for joint speech-text modeling, with detailed architecture and training configuration that support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The tokenization depends on ASR transcriptions from Whisper, and the paper assumes sufficient ASR quality without analyzing robustness to ASR errors; this is a potential vulnerability because alignment errors or ASR mistakes could degrade both tokenization and downstream SLM performance.

The word-level grouping/averaging/alignment procedure is heuristic and may discard temporal and fine-grained paralinguistic information; it is not ablated, and its sensitivity to ASR tokenization and LLM tokenization mismatches is not investigated.

The spoken language modeling evaluation is primarily likelihood-based classification on SALMON and StoryCloze, not direct generation quality. The paper claims natural speech and text continuation, but does not report human evaluation or synthesis metrics such as WER, UTMOS, speaker similarity, or emotion preservation on generated continuations.

Ablations are limited: there is no systematic study of the specialized cross-attention aggregation, ASR initialization, RVQ depth/codebook size, LoRA rank, word-level averaging vs. alternatives, or full fine-tuning vs. LoRA. The source of gains is therefore not fully isolated.

The results are competitive but not consistently superior: TASLM is below Spirit LM Expr. on several SALMON acoustic metrics, and still notably below the ASR+LLM cascade on StoryCloze. No statistical significance tests or error bars are provided, and benchmark subset details are sparse.
Efficiency benefits are often asserted rather than quantified; the paper does not report training/inference time, memory usage, or throughput improvements relative to baselines.
The UTMOS score exceeding ground-truth UTMOS is unusual and not discussed; this may indicate metric unreliability or evaluation artifacts that warrant explanation.

The work builds on several existing components (Distil-Whisper, CosyVoice S3 units, MELLE-style latent modeling, LoRA) and the novelty is mainly in their combination and alignment strategy, so the contribution may be viewed as incremental unless the alignment mechanism and reconstruction objective are more thoroughly analyzed.

strengths: Addresses an important problem in joint speech-text spoken language modeling: the modality and length mismatch between speech tokens and text tokens. The proposed text-aligned tokenization is intuitive and directly targets this issue.

Introduces a clean attention-based aggregation mechanism that uses text tokens as queries and speech encoder representations as keys/values, enabling text-aligned speech tokenization without explicit forced alignment.

Provides extensive empirical evaluation across multiple settings: speech reconstruction, text-aligned speech editing, speech continuation, SALMON/StoryCloze likelihood benchmarks, and spoken question answering. Comparisons include strong SLM baselines such as TWIST, Spirit LM, Moshi, and cascade systems.

Achieves strong reconstruction quality at a very low speech-token bitrate (~150 bps), with high MOS scores and preserved paralinguistic information. The text-aligned editing demonstration is compelling, even if qualitative.

The TASLM results are promising: a 1B-parameter model outperforms much larger pretrained SLMs on speech continuation under both human and GPT-4o/UTMOS evaluations, and it does not degrade its base text LLM on spoken QA, supporting the usefulness of text-aligned joint modeling.
Reproducibility is generally good: training details, hyperparameters, standard deviations, human-evaluation instructions, and released code/model/demo are provided.
weaknesses: The inference procedure for spoken language modeling is not fully clear. TASTE tokenization requires a text transcription, so for speech continuation and spoken QA it is unclear whether ground-truth text, ASR output, or generated text tokens are used for the speech prompt/question. If text is provided or obtained by an external ASR system, comparisons to speech-only SLMs may be unfair, and the method is not a fully speech-only or end-to-end system.

The reported bitrate for TASTE likely accounts only for the speech tokens, but the decoder also conditions on text tokens. Thus TASTE is not a standalone speech codec; the overall representation includes both text and speech tokens. This should be acknowledged and ideally included in bitrate/latency comparisons.

Technical novelty is somewhat limited: the core mechanism combines a frozen Whisper encoder, cross-attention with text as queries, RVQ, and a pretrained CosyVoice decoder. The central idea of using text tokens as attention queries is straightforward, and the claim of being the 'first end-to-end' reconstruction-based text-aligned tokenizer is weakened by the ASR-text dependency.

The text-aligned speech editing evaluation is only qualitative (alignment plots and demo examples), with no objective metrics or controlled user study to quantify editing accuracy, naturalness, or paralinguistic transfer.

Some evaluations rely on small human-listening samples (e.g., 20 samples with >10 ratings each) and GPT-4o MOS scoring text relevance after ASR rather than direct acoustic quality. More detailed protocol analysis, inter-annotator agreement, and larger-scale evaluation would strengthen the claims.

The method is evaluated only on English data, and limitations such as no streaming, turn-taking, or instruction-following are acknowledged but not explored. Robustness to ASR errors and noisy/domain-shifted speech is also not analyzed.

strengths: The paper tackles an important problem in spoken language modeling: the length mismatch between speech and text tokens for joint modeling.
The proposed TASTE tokenizer is conceptually simple and plausible: using text tokens as queries to aggregate Whisper encoder states, followed by RVQ and reconstruction training.
The reported reconstruction results are promising under the stated setup, with high MOS predictions, speaker similarity, and MUSHRA at a low reported speech-token rate.
The TASLM experiments show that a 1B model can be efficiently adapted with LoRA and achieve strong speech-continuation and StoryCloze results relative to several prior SLMs.
The paper includes useful appendix material with training details, human-evaluation prompts, and standard deviations.
The text-aligned speech editing demonstration is an interesting qualitative use case.
weaknesses: The central low-bitrate reconstruction claim is not fairly evaluated: TASTE's decoder receives the ground-truth text transcription, while Encodec, SpeechTokenizer, and Mimi are textless codecs. The reported ~150 bps excludes the text side information, so it is not comparable to textless speech-coding bitrates and is more like text-conditioned reconstruction/TTS.

The SALMON comparison is mischaracterized as comparable: TASLM (token) scores 60.8 versus Spirit LM Expr. 69.0, and the detailed table shows lower acoustic-consistency accuracy on most subtasks. The overall average masks this regression.

Several technical details are unclear or missing: how the shallow encoder layer is selected, the aggregator architecture/depth, how discrete RVQ codes are word-grouped and aligned with LLM subword tokens, how prompt transcriptions are obtained at inference, and how text and speech tokens are jointly sampled while maintaining alignment. Algorithm 1 also has inconsistent notation.

Novelty is incremental: text-speech cross-attention has precedent in TTS style control, and the method relies heavily on frozen Whisper, a pre-trained S3 tokenizer/vocoder, and a reconstruction objective. The 'first end-to-end' claim is overstated.

Baseline comparisons are not fully controlled. TASLM uses LoRA while some baselines may use different fine-tuning or base LLMs; the S3-token joint-modeling baseline is poorly specified; there is no same-base text-only LLM continuation baseline; and Q&A compares a pre-trained TASLM to instruction-finetuned systems under an underspecified few-shot setup.
Speech editing is evaluated only qualitatively, with no objective or human evaluation of prosody transfer, naturalness, or robustness.

Some claims rely on automated MOS metrics that can be gamed or biased; TASTE's UTMOS/DNSMOS exceeding ground truth is suspicious and should be analyzed rather than presented as straightforwardly positive.
Reproducibility is incomplete: the code/model link is absent, and several hyperparameters and training protocols are not specified.
Dependence on ASR text at tokenization time may limit streaming, low-latency, and true 'listen-and-speak' use; the limitation section does not adequately address this fundamental dependency.
Statistical significance of improvements is not established sufficiently, especially given high variance and inconsistent behavior across benchmarks.

strengths: Introduces TASTE, a novel text-aligned speech tokenization/embedding method that directly mitigates the length mismatch for joint speech-text spoken language modeling by aligning speech tokens with ASR transcription via a cross-attention aggregator and RVQ quantizer.

Achieves high-quality speech reconstruction at an extremely low bitrate (~150 bps), with competitive MOS/MUSHRA scores and much better similarity than a text-only baseline; also demonstrates a useful text-aligned speech editing application.

Enables straightforward joint spoken language modeling by LoRA fine-tuning a text LLM; TASLM 1B outperforms larger pre-trained SLMs on speech continuation across GPT-4o, UTMOS, and human MOS, and achieves strong likelihood-based benchmark results.

Evaluation is extensive: reconstruction quality/similarity, speech continuation, SALMON/StoryCloze likelihood benchmarks, spoken question answering, human listening tests, and reported standard deviations.
The paper is clearly written, well-positioned against prior work, and includes sufficient training details and limitations for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The text alignment is ultimately word-level via averaging and repetition to handle ASR-vs-LLM vocabulary mismatch, rather than a direct token-level alignment; this may discard fine-grained paralinguistic detail and makes the central 'text-aligned' claim less precise.

There is no systematic ablation over key design choices, including RVQ layers, codebook size, choice of encoder layers for keys/values, aggregator architecture, loss weights, and word-level versus token-level alignment, making it hard to attribute gains to individual components.

Evaluation is limited to English; robustness to ASR errors, multilingual settings, noisy/spontaneous speech, and different transcription qualities is not explored, despite the method's dependence on ASR transcripts.

On several reconstruction metrics (WER, ViSQOL, duration consistency), TASTE trails codec and S3-token baselines, and the MUSHRA test uses a modest number of samples/evaluators; the bitrate is estimated rather than measured under a fixed codec.
Spoken QA and SALMON acoustic consistency results are not state-of-the-art and lag some larger models, and the model does not support streaming or robust instruction following.

The method relies on frozen Whisper large-v3 and pseudo-labeled/ground-truth transcriptions during training; the impact of ASR error propagation on tokenization and downstream SLM performance is not analyzed.
